paras: The lynching of Frank McManus took place in Minneapolis, Minnesota, before dawn on April 28, 1882, when fifty to sixty disguised men broke into the Hennepin County jail, took McManus from his cell and hanged him from a tree near the High School. McManus had been arrested the day before, accused of raping a four-year-old girl. A coroner's jury found that he died 'by means unknown to the jury', and a judge's call for indictments followed, while much of the press approved the killing.

On the afternoon of April 27, according to the St. Paul Daily Globe, a man bought candy for Minnie Spear, the four-year-old daughter of Jason P. Spear, at a store on Eleventh street and led her away. The child was later found in bushes, badly injured, and three physicians judged her recovery doubtful. Officer William Gleason ran down a man on Fourth avenue south and took him to the police station, where he was booked on a charge of rape.

The prisoner gave his name as Frank or John McManniss, said he came from Boston, and was described as about 26 with a scarred face. Police Chief A. S. Munger later testified that the man confessed to him, and the Globe said he admitted his guilt to another officer. As crowds gathered that evening, he was moved to the county jail about 10:30 p.m. and placed in the charge of Sheriff J. M. Eustis.

About 1 a.m. they forced the jail door, and Eustis testified that four or five disguised men held him in a corner after he refused them entry. When the sheriff would not give up the keys or name the cell, the men broke cell doors with sledges and timbers for about three hours until they found the prisoner in cell No. 3 on the third tier.

Handcuffed, he was marched to the Spear house, where Mrs. Snyder, Mrs. Smith and Mrs. Powell identified him as the man they had seen with the child. He was then taken to an oak at the corner of Fourth avenue and Twelfth street, across from the High School, where, according to the Northern Pacific Farmer's account, he gave his name as Tim Cromley of South Boston and confessed after first denying the crime. He was hanged about 4 a.m., and the band scattered at a cry of police, leaving the body hanging, where Officer Caswell saw it about 7 o'clock.

Coroner A. C. Fairbairn held an inquest on April 29, and the jury found that McManus died of strangulation 'by means unknown to the jury', a verdict the Globe called 'agreeable to the popular feeling'. A witness from South Boston identified the body as Frank McManus, and the Boston Herald traced his family there, though a brother doubted the identification.
On May 9 Judge Lochren charged the Hennepin County grand jury to indict everyone connected with the lynching, reportedly for murder. No report of an indictment or trial was found in the coverage.

The Globe, which carried the first local reports, headlined the crime 'Deed of a Demon' and insisted the lynchers were vigilantes, 'not a rabble nor a mob'. A letter signed 'Law Abider' answered a Pioneer Press critic of the sheriff by calling the lynchers 'men of influence, means and respectability'. The Associated Press dispatch, datelined St. Paul, called McManus a tramp and said public sentiment was 'indisputably' with the lynchers.

That wire ran on April 28 and 29 in papers from Memphis and Rock Island to Sacramento, and condensed versions reached Tennessee and Kentucky weeklies in early May. Short summaries garbled the details, placing the lynching in St. Paul or naming the man Francis McManus or Frank Warner. A Raleigh paper added that he had once served time for outraging two Black girls and that the child had died, claims not found elsewhere.

Editorial comment was largely approving: the Superior Times was 'not disposed to find fault', and the Mankato Free Press quoted a Stillwater minister calling the lynching right. Dissent was muted, as a Globe reader called it 'a great moral wrong' that nearly every man defended, and the Worthington Advance later noted that child rapes continued after it.
Accounts differ on the size of the band, fifty in the Globe and sixty in the wire, and on the time of the hanging, from 3:57 to 4:15 a.m.

accounts.label: Globe Minneapolis correspondent
accounts.gist: A planned committee of about fifty citizens, disguised with handkerchiefs, broke into the jail over three hours, had the man identified, and hanged him after he confessed.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Masked men made the sheriff prisoner, broke open cells floor by floor, took McManus to his victim's house, and hanged him at 4:15 a.m. after he confessed.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Officers testified to the arrest, an alleged confession, and the removal by disguised men; the jury found strangulation by means unknown.

accounts.label: Boston Herald inquiry
accounts.gist: Traced a Frank McManus of South Boston, a rolling-mill worker; his brother doubted the identification.

framing.detail: The Globe headlined 'Deed of a Demon' and called the lynchers vigilantes, 'not a rabble nor a mob', who acted 'with system'.
A 'Law Abider' letter called them 'law abiding citizens, men of influence, means and respectability'.
The AP wire ran as 'A Wretch Strung Up' and 'Lynch Law' and said public sentiment was with the lynchers.
The Superior Times was 'not disposed to find fault' and the Mankato Free Press quoted a minister calling it right.
Judge Lochren, as reported, 'severely denounced' the lynching.
A Globe reader called it 'a great moral wrong' that nearly every man defended; the Worthington Advance doubted that lynching deterred rape.

versions.value: Tim Cromley / Crowley / Crawley (his own last statement)

conflicts.note: The inquest identified the body as Frank McManus (A11); the Boston Herald thought he took the Crowley name from a boxer known to his brother (A24).
The St. Paul placings come from brief summaries that misread the St. Paul dateline; local reports and the inquest put it in Minneapolis.
The sheriff's sworn testimony gives about 4 o'clock (A11).
The Raleigh paper's claim stands alone; later wire reports say she was improving.
